  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 4 ## From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360 In Chapter 3, I traced the increasingly widespread association of mucus with Wind disorders from the tenth to the twelfth century and showed that several illnesses whose pathomechanisms had been considered close to those of kuang—Wind strokes and xian 痈 seizures—were often treated with anti-mucus remedies by the end of that period. Let me now explain how the mucus-and-Fire etiology of madness that dominated late-imperial conceptions of insanity developed. The mucus-and-Fire script emerged among doctrinally minded physicians who lived in north China under the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), and was consolidated by southern doctors who were influenced by these northerners in the early fourteenth century under the Yuan dynasty (1260-1368), after the Mongol conquest of both the Jin and the southern Song (1127-1279) had re-established contacts between north and south China. The innovations these medical thinkers proposed built on the trends I outlined in Chapter 3, but it was their doctrinal and therapeutic precepts that came to dominate later medical thinking.
